Character and location of back pain (mid-back pain is concerning for thoracic cord involvement)
Associated symptoms: numbness, tingling, saddle anesthesia, urinary retention or incontinence, fecal incontinence
Functional status: ability to walk, stand, or transfer
Recent falls or trauma
Previous similar symptoms
General: Assess for distress, ability to move
Neurological exam:
Motor strength in lower extremities (graded 0-5)
Sensory exam: light touch, pinprick, proprioception in lower extremities and perineum
Reflexes: patellar, Achilles (may be brisk below the level of compression)
Babinski sign (upgoing plantar reflex suggests upper motor neuron lesion)
Tone (spasticity may be present)
Gait (if safe)
Rectal exam: anal tone, perianal sensation
Bladder scan for urinary retention (post-void residual >100 mL is suggestive)
Assess ability to ambulate safely
Diagnostic Performance Data:
Sensitivity of clinical findings for spinal cord compression is variable:
Back pain: present in >90% of cases
Motor weakness: present in ~60-85%
Sensory changes: ~50-80%
Bladder/bowel dysfunction: ~20-50% at presentation
Loss of rectal tone and perianal sensation are specific but not sensitive for cauda equina syndrome
MRI is the gold standard for diagnosis (sensitivity >90%)
Key findings: new weakness, sensory changes, sphincter dysfunction, midline back pain in a patient with metastatic cancer

raw.prompt: Given this presentation, what history, physical examination, and bedside tests should I perform? Include any diagnostic performance data you know.
raw.text:
This presentation is concerning for possible spinal cord compression, a medical emergency in patients with metastatic cancer.

**History:**
- Onset, duration, and progression of leg weakness and heaviness
- Character and location of back pain (mid-back pain is concerning for thoracic cord involvement)
- Associated symptoms: numbness, tingling, saddle anesthesia, urinary retention or incontinence, fecal incontinence
- Functional status: ability to walk, stand, or transfer
- Recent falls or trauma
- Previous similar symptoms

**Physical Examination:**
- General: Assess for distress, ability to move
- Neurological exam:
  - Motor strength in lower extremities (graded 0-5)
  - Sensory exam: light touch, pinprick, proprioception in lower extremities and perineum
  - Reflexes: patellar, Achilles (may be brisk below the level of compression)
  - Babinski sign (upgoing plantar reflex suggests upper motor neuron lesion)
  - Tone (spasticity may be present)
  - Gait (if safe)
  - Rectal exam: anal tone, perianal sensation

**Bedside Tests:**
- Bladder scan for urinary retention (post-void residual >100 mL is suggestive)
- Assess ability to ambulate safely

**Diagnostic Performance Data:**
- Sensitivity of clinical findings for spinal cord compression is variable:
  - Back pain: present in >90% of cases
  - Motor weakness: present in ~60-85%
  - Sensory changes: ~50-80%
  - Bladder/bowel dysfunction: ~20-50% at presentation
- Loss of rectal tone and perianal sensation are specific but not sensitive for cauda equina syndrome.
- MRI is the gold standard for diagnosis (sensitivity >90%).

**Summary:**
- This is a clinical emergency. Prompt recognition and MRI are critical. Early corticosteroids may be indicated after diagnosis is suspected.
- Key findings: new weakness, sensory changes, sphincter dysfunction, midline back pain in a patient with metastatic cancer.

**References:**
- Loblaw DA, Perry J, Chambers A, Laperriere NJ. Systematic review of the diagnosis and management of malignant extradural spinal cord compression. JCO 2005.
- Greenberg MS. Handbook of Neurosurgery, 9th Edition.
